title: Requested payments and what followed
question: After an organization paid money at an official’s request, did the Board of Supervisors or a commission decide something that named it within a year?
finding: Of 170 payments of $1,000 or more that organizations made at a City official’s request (2013 to late 2025), 9 were followed within a year by a Board or commission decision naming the payor, and 7 were preceded by one in the year before. For requests by State officials the figures are 62 followed and 57 preceded, of 1,805. Decisions are about as common after a payment as before it. In 1 of them the official who asked was also a sponsor of the later Board file: Pacific Gas & Electric Co paid $5,000 at the request of Malia Cohen on 2017-08-11, and 133 days later the Board passed “Grant of Easement - Pacific Gas and Electric Company - 68.25 Square Feet at Nort”.
how: Requested (“behested”) payments come from three files: City officers’ reports, the older City elected-officer reports, and State officers’ reports that touch San Francisco. For each payor that is an organization, three records were searched for its name: the counterparty of any contract, lease or agreement the Board passed (grants the City accepted and legal settlements are left out), the titles and stated project sponsors of the Board’s land-use files, and applicants in the minutes of the smaller commissions. A decision counts if it fell in the 365 days after the payment; the same search over the 365 days before is the comparison. The sponsor test uses the sponsors printed on the Board file. In the table, payments at City officials’ request are listed one by one; payments at State officials’ request are folded into one row for each payor and decision.
limits: The report exists because the official disclosed it. Large companies and institutions are named in Board files every year, so a decision within a year is expected for them whether or not they gave; the before-and-after comparison shows how much. Several of the City rows are grantees paying on at a department head’s request, where the later decision is their own grant. A name on a Board file does not mean the decision favoured the payor. Planning Commission minutes print addresses, not applicants, so they could not be searched. State officials do not vote on City files. This extends the list of requested payments in the “interests” results by adding the decisions; it does not repeat that list. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
